title: Detection of Identify Business Tempo
summary: This detection strategy covers the reconnaissance technique of identifying business tempo, where an adversary learns when an organization is busy, when staff are away, and when change or payment cycles happen. It matters because an intrusion launched during a holiday period or a major event is far less likely to be noticed in time, and because payroll and finance cycles tell an attacker when a fraudulent payment will look normal. The telemetry that makes detection possible is mail gateway and calendar metadata, virtual private network and identity provider sign in logs with time patterns, and public profile or website change monitoring. The main failure mode is that the collection often happens entirely on public sources such as social media and press releases, so the rule can only catch the parts that touch your own systems.

beginner.definition: This detection looks for signs that someone is studying the daily rhythm of your company. Business tempo means the normal times when work happens, such as office hours, pay days, and holiday periods. Attackers want this so they can act when few people are watching. The rule watches for unusual bursts of questions about your working hours and staff absence.
beginner.whyItMatters: An attack during a quiet period is noticed later, which gives the attacker more time. Knowing your pay cycle helps a fake invoice look normal. Learning who is on leave helps an attacker pick a target whose account will not be checked. These questions often come before any real intrusion, so they are a useful warning.
howItWorks: The mail gateway records inbound messages, including ones that ask about opening hours.
The identity provider records every sign in with a timestamp and a country or region.
The rule builds a normal picture of sign in times for each team and each region.
It flags accounts that sign in at unusual hours or from new countries.
Public monitoring shows when your website or social profiles are scraped in bulk.
A pattern of staff absence questions plus odd hour sign ins raises an alert for review.
beginner.example: Picture a shop that keeps a door log and a staff rota. A person may ask when the shop is quietest. That person then visits only at those times and never buys anything. This is worth watching. The rota and the door log together show the pattern. Neither record alone would be enough.
takeaways: The signal is a combination of absence questions and unusual sign in times.
Public sources are where most tempo collection happens, so coverage is limited.
A baseline of normal working hours per team is required before alerts are useful.

objectives: Define business tempo and explain why attackers study it.
Identify the internal logs that show tempo collection activity.
Write a rule that flags sign ins outside a learned working pattern.
Explain how calendar and out of office data can be misused.
Describe the limits of detection when the source is public information.
dataSources: Identity provider sign in logs recording user, source address, country, client application and timestamp
Virtual private network authentication logs with session start and end times per user account
Email security gateway logs showing inbound enquiries about opening hours, holidays or staff availability
Web server and social platform monitoring records showing bulk retrieval of organization pages and profiles
logic: The pattern is an external party asking repeatedly about organization working hours, holiday closures, or named staff availability, combined with sign in activity from organization accounts outside the hours that the account normally uses. The fields that must be correlated are the user or sender, the source address and country, the timestamp against the account baseline, and the volume of questions about schedule or absence. The malicious case is a burst of scheduling questions from one new contact followed by account access at three in the morning from an unfamiliar region. The benign case is a genuine supplier scheduling deliveries or a staff member working late during a known release period.
pseudoQuery:
# title: Account Sign In Outside Learned Working Hours
# logsource:
#   product: azure
#   service: signinlogs
# detection:
#   selection:
#     ResultType: '0'
#     UserPrincipalName|endswith: '@example[.]com'
#   filter_expected:
#     UserPrincipalName|contains:
#       - 'build-service@'
#       - 'oncall-'
#   condition: selection and not filter_expected | count() by UserPrincipalName > 5 within 2h
# level: low
falsePositives: Staff who regularly work outside office hours because they support customers in other time zones
Automated service accounts that sign in on a fixed schedule around the clock
Travel to a conference or holiday that changes a user location and working hours for a short period
tuningNotes: First learn the normal sign in window per user and per team over at least a month, and filter service accounts, on call rota accounts, and known travel periods inside the rule. Scope the alert to privileged roles and to finance or payroll staff, where the impact of quiet period activity is greatest, and raise priority when an unusual sign in follows a burst of scheduling enquiries. The coverage you lose is the public side of tempo collection, which you cannot see at all, so keep an external monitoring process for brand and profile scraping.
